result.summary: Pindar praises Sogenes of Aigina, a victor in the pentathlon at Nemea, beginning with a prayer to Eileithuia. He discusses poetry's power to preserve fame, defends himself against the charge of slighting Neoptolemos, and ends with a prayer to Herakles for Sogenes' house.

scenes.title: Editorial introduction
scenes.summary: A note gives the probable date and says the ode is full of obscure allusions, including a defence of Pindar over Neoptolemos.

scenes.title: Prayer to Eileithuia and song
scenes.summary: Pindar invokes Eileithuia, goddess of childbirth, credits her for Sogenes' victory, and says song gives deeds lasting fame.
scenes.stakes: Great deeds fall into darkness if no song records them.

scenes.title: Odysseus, Homer and Aias
scenes.summary: Pindar suspects Homer made Odysseus' fame exceed his deeds, while Aias killed himself over the arms of Achilles.
scenes.stakes: Aias lost his life through the blindness of men's judgment.

scenes.title: Death of Neoptolemos at Pytho
scenes.summary: Neoptolemos, after Troy and a spell as king in Molossia, is killed at Delphi in a quarrel over meat and becomes guardian of the sanctuary.

scenes.title: Human lot and Pindar's defence
scenes.summary: Pindar praises Aigina and Thearion, says perfect bliss is impossible for men, and defends the honesty of his praise.
scenes.stakes: Pindar's reputation against the charge of slander.

scenes.title: Hymn to Zeus and Herakles
scenes.summary: Pindar honours Zeus, Aiakos and Herakles, prays for Sogenes' family, and denies having wronged Neoptolemos.

alias_notes.explanation: Pytho is the older name of Delphi, seat of Apollo's oracle.
Epithet for Athena, not named in this translation.

notable_quotes.reason: Pindar states that deeds need song to escape darkness.
Memorable statement that perfect bliss is impossible for mortals.

analysis.text: Poetry confers lasting fame on deeds, but Pindar warns that praise must be truthful and that human fortune is always limited.
The ode shows Aigina's pride in the Aiakidai and the political sensitivity of Pindar's relation to Delphi and Neoptolemos' cult.

legacy.text: Pindar's doubt that Homer inflated Odysseus' fame is an early example of Greek criticism of poetic reputation.

fun_facts.text: Neoptolemos' tomb at Delphi was a hero cult site, which explains Pindar's concern with how he portrayed him.

language_notes.text: Moirai are the Fates; "hearken" means listen, and "thou" and "sittest" are archaic second-person forms.
Hebe, goddess of youth, is called Eileithuia's sister; to come "unto" her means to reach youthful vigour.
"Not all for a like life": humans are given breath but not equal fortunes; each is bound to a separate portion by fate.
The "five-game prize" is the pentathlon, the five-event contest in which Sogenes won.
The sons of Aiakos are the Aiginetans, whose legendary ancestor Aiakos was king of Aigina; "fain" means eager.
Mnemosyne is Memory, mother of the Muses; her "shining fillet" is a bright headband.
The shipmates' wisdom is to wait patiently for a fair wind and not squander goods out of greed; the point is moderation.
Odysseus' "winged craft" refers to his cunning tales in Homer; "feigning" means invention, so Pindar suspects exaggeration.
Aias killed himself after the arms of Achilles went to Odysseus; Menelaos' bride was Helen, and Ilos' town is Troy.
The "centre-stone" is the omphalos at Delphi, so Pindar speaks of those who have gone to Delphi.
Pytho is the older name for Delphi, site of Apollo's oracle and sanctuary. Danaoi is Homer's name for the Greeks.
"Missed Skyros": storms drove his ships off course, so he never reached the island and instead went overland and by sea to Epirus (Ephyra, Molossia).
"Entertainers of strangers" means hosts, the Delphians who welcomed visitors. "Sons of Aiakos" means descendants of Aiakos; Neoptolemos was his great-grandson.
A proxeny was the office of a public friend and host of a foreign city. Pindar was proxenos of Aigina's friends, so he trusts the goodwill of his hosts.
The javelin image: the ode is thrown as a cast that stays within the line. The wrestler's "sweatless" neck suggests praise that comes before exertion or hardship.
Gold, ivory and a lily from the sea suggest precious materials in the poet's garland of song; the "deep sea's dew" evokes Aigina's island setting.
The "conqueror of the giants" is Herakles, who fought beside the gods against the giants. Sogenes' house stands near his shrines.
The proverb "Korinthos son of Zeus" mocked tedious repetition of a stale boast. Pindar says he will not retell the same tale.

context_notes.text: Neoptolemos, son of Achilles, was said to have been killed at Delphi; Pindar's treatment of this episode had apparently offended Aiginetans.
Eileithuia was the goddess who presided over childbirth and was thought to help women in labour.
Aias (Ajax) was a great Greek warrior at Troy, second only to Achilles in strength, and killed himself out of anger.
Neoptolemos, son of Achilles, brought Trojan spoils to Apollo's shrine. Other accounts of his death at Delphi differ, and Pindar gives his own version.
Aigina, a nymph and island, was loved by Zeus and bore Aiakos. The Aiakidai were its heroic family.
Thearion is the father of Sogenes, the victorious boy athlete honoured by this ode.
Nemea hosted games for Zeus. Aiakos, Zeus's son, ruled Aigina, and his descendants Peleus and Telamon were friends of Herakles.

literary_notes.text: Pindar addresses the goddess directly in the opening prayer, giving the ode a solemn, ritual tone.
Song is a stream and a mirror: it flows from the Muses and reflects noble deeds so they are not lost.
Pindar, himself a poet, suspects the persuasive power of poetry, noting that Homer's art can make fame outweigh deeds.
Death is a wave that falls on everyone, famed or unknown, which stresses that only fame distinguishes them.
Pindar states a general truth about human limits, a maxim that tempers praise of Sogenes with reminder of mortality.
Praise is compared to streams of water, as refreshing and flowing freely to the worthy, while slander is kept away.
His swift words are likened to a bronze-headed javelin, giving the song force and accuracy.
The house standing among Herakles' shrines is compared to a four-horse team, with a shrine on each side, suggesting balance and divine protection.
Pindar speaks directly to Herakles as a blessed spirit, turning the ode into prayer.
